title: Five cells, four steps
hook: Every cell only counts its neighbours. Watch what five cells do in four steps.

knows: a grid of cells, each live or empty
a neighbour is one of the 8 cells touching a cell
doesNotKnow: that tiny local rules can make a pattern that travels

misconception: Simple rules about neighbours can only make simple, static or dying patterns.
objective: The learner can explain that a glider keeps 5 live cells every step, that its shape returns after 4 steps one cell right and one down, and that no rule says to move.

claims.text: A glider has 5 live cells at every generation from 0 to 4, and at generation 4 it is the generation-0 shape moved one cell right and one cell down.
claims.source: Builder's node script: glider (1,0) (2,1) (0,2) (1,2) (2,2) (x right, y down), rule live-with-2-or-3-lives, empty-with-exactly-3-born, else dies; live counts 5,5,5,5,5; generation 4 = (2,1) (3,2) (1,3) (2,3) (3,3) = generation 0 shifted by (+1,+1). The stage places the glider at offset (1,1) on a 7x7 grid so it never meets the edge. TheAlgorithms/Python used only as a reference; no code copied.

claims.text: In the first step two cells die (the glider's cells with only 1 live neighbour) and two cells are born (empty cells with exactly 3 live neighbours); the other three live cells stay.
claims.source: Builder's node script, gen 0 to gen 1 in the glider's own coordinates: (1,0) has 1 live neighbour and dies; (0,2) has 1 and dies; (2,1) has 3, (1,2) has 3 and (2,2) has 2 and live on; (0,1) and (1,3) have exactly 3 and are born. Stage neighbour counts come from the same function.

claims.text: The rule is: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive, an empty cell with exactly 3 live neighbours comes alive, and every other cell dies or stays empty; this is Conway's Game of Life, and the five-cell pattern is called a glider.
claims.source: Gardner, M. (1970), 'Mathematical Games: The fantastic combinations of John Conway's new solitaire game "life"', Scientific American, October 1970.

claims.text: Patterns in Conway's Game of Life can be built to compute anything a computer can.
claims.source: Berlekamp, Conway and Guy, Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays, 1982, ch. 25 (a Life computer built from gliders and guns; Life is Turing complete).

claims.text: No rule says move: each cell only counts its neighbours, and the pattern travels.
claims.source: The rule in Demo.tsx step() reads only a cell's own state and its 8 neighbours; no cell or pattern has a position or velocity. Travel is the observed generation-4 result in c1.

recall.question: In Conway's Game of Life no rule says 'move'. Why does a glider still travel across the grid?
options: Each step the neighbour-count rule rebuilds the same shape one cell over after 4 steps
Each live cell remembers which way to walk
The grid slides under the pattern
recall.why: Cells only count live neighbours. Applied step after step, that rule gives the glider back after 4 generations shifted one cell right and one down.
